summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar to change a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in force since 2007. What that protection reaches in practice is not set out in the sources: whether it covers service refusal, harassment, goods and facilities, or only employment is unresolved here.

Criminal-law protection runs on a separate footing and has moved further. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime, with assent on 25 September and commencement on 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending the hate crime and hate speech legislation to add protections for transgender identity, giving gender identity its own footing in the criminal law for the first time. A companion bill passed the same month makes it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Official response to anti-gay hostility has been stated at ministerial level. After an incident of anti-gay abuse, the Ministry for Justice and Equality said in July 2021 that it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what it called disgusting lurking homophobia; the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, used the same phrase of abuse directed at social media during Pride month, and the Justice Ministry began investigating a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence.

Family and partnership recognition is established rather than contested. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014 and same-sex marriage since December 2016, when the bill passed unanimously following a December 2015 consultation that had left the population divided; the draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act went before Parliament in August 2016 after an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, popular consultation and the main parties indicated support. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 breached the Gibraltar Constitution, after a long-term lesbian couple refused an adoption challenged the restriction; the law was amended through the 2014 civil-partnership legislation, and the Adoption Act 2023, in full effect from 18 April 2024, expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt. Altruistic non-commercial surrogacy has been permitted for married couples and civil partners since February 2021, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived by artificial insemination, and the Gibraltar Health Authority extended assisted reproduction to lesbian couples in June 2017. A trans visitor travelling with a partner or children should not expect family status to be the source of difficulty; identity documents are.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender, set by the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011 after the Supreme Court held on 8 April 2011 that the former age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional; the equalised age took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009.

Oversight comes from outside as well as within. The United Kingdom House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2007-08 report on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar, and its 2008 inquiry recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal across all overseas territories.
tangentialFactors:
The United Kingdom's equality framework does not reach Gibraltar automatically. The Equality Act 2010 and the 2025 single-sex-services code, which together govern service access and facility rules in the parent jurisdiction, apply to Gibraltar only through an Order in Council, and no such instrument is on record. A visitor who has encountered those rules in the United Kingdom should not assume the same text governs here.

The two strands of protection have developed at different speeds. Discrimination law has stood largely unchanged in substance since 2007, while the criminal law has been amended twice in thirteen years, most recently in July 2026 to carry gender identity expressly. The result is a jurisdiction where a trans person's strongest statutory footing is in the criminal statutes rather than in the equality statutes.

Public and political temperature is a live variable. The Ministry for Justice and Equality's July 2021 statement on anti-gay abuse, and the Chief Minister's description of social-media abuse during Pride month as disgusting lurking homophobia, indicate that hostile speech has been visible enough to draw a ministerial response, and that the government's stated posture is to legislate against it.

Family law is the least likely source of friction for a visitor travelling with a partner or children. Same-sex marriage, civil partnership, joint adoption, altruistic surrogacy and assisted reproduction for lesbian couples are all settled and in operation, which places Gibraltar ahead of several comparable small jurisdictions on recognition while leaving it behind on document amendment.
localsOnly:
Residents have had discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation and gender reassignment since 2007, and hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation since October 2013. The July 2026 bill extends the hate crime and hate speech provisions to transgender identity, and the companion bill of the same month creates an offence of offering or practising conversion therapy.

Residents can enter a civil partnership from 2014 and a same-sex marriage from December 2016, adopt as a same-sex couple under the Adoption Act 2023 in force from 18 April 2024, use altruistic non-commercial surrogacy under the February 2021 law, and access assisted reproduction through the Gibraltar Health Authority's policy amended in June 2017 to include lesbian couples.

Residents face the same gender-recognition gap as visitors: no route exists to change a legal gender marker, so the restriction falls on people living here as well as on those passing through. The equal age of consent of 16 has applied since 23 November 2012 following the Supreme Court's ruling of 8 April 2011.

The Ministry for Justice and Equality has undertaken to consider legislation against homophobic abuse, and in July 2021 began examining a proposal to make denigration on the basis of sexual orientation a specific offence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The practical scope of the 2007 discrimination protection is unresolved. The sources confirm that sexual orientation and gender reassignment are protected grounds but do not say whether the protection reaches service refusal, harassment, access to goods and facilities, or only employment.

Commencement of the July 2026 measures is unresolved. The sources record that Parliament passed the bill adding transgender identity to the hate crime and hate speech legislation and the companion bill criminalising conversion therapy, but do not record assent dates or entry into force.

Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is unresolved; the sourced material contains no such instrument, and absence of a record is not the same as a confirmed negative.

Enforcement of the 2013 sexual-orientation hate-crime provision, and any enforcement of the 2026 gender-identity provisions, is not sourced: no prosecution figures, charging guidance or police practice are available here. Border and document-screening practice for trans travellers arriving in Gibraltar is likewise not sourced.

Whether any gender-recognition bill or policy is under consideration in Gibraltar is not sourced; the inventory records only that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender.
